warmup.q: A thread holds the read lock of a ReentrantReadWriteLock. Then it calls writeLock().lock() on the same lock. No other thread touches the lock. What happens?
options: It gets the write lock at once, because it is the only reader
It waits forever: the write lock waits for every reader to leave, and this thread is one of them
It gets the write lock and quietly drops its read lock
warmup.why: ReentrantReadWriteLock can't turn a read lock into a write lock. The write lock needs zero readers, and the thread's own read lock counts, so the thread parks and never wakes. Nothing throws, and, as the third section shows, a thread dump doesn't even report it as a deadlock. Kotlin's write { } helper behaves differently, and the comparison near the end shows how.

opening:
Picture the bank at the end of the day. A batch job, a program that works through a long list in one go, adds the day's interest to every account. It runs on its own thread, one line of work among several in the program. For a second and a half, it holds the lock on the ledger, the bank's book of balances. A lock lets one thread at a time in.

Just then, a customer at a cash machine asks for her balance. With synchronized, her request joins the line for the lock and stays there. It can't give up after 200 ms and ask her to try again, and even a shutdown can't call it back. So she watches a spinning wheel the whole time.

Deadlock, livelock and starvation ended with a lock that can give up. ReentrantLock is that lock, and switching takes one line. It's almost too easy: unlike synchronized, it never lets go by itself.

In this lesson, we'll wait for a busy lock three ways, give each kind of waiting thread its own waiting room, and let readers share a lock, or skip it. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a customer at a cash machine, watching a spinning wheel while the interest job held the ledger. ReentrantLock let her request give up after 200 ms. Condition gave the kitchen's waiters and cooks a waiting room each. The read-write lock let readers share the rate table, as long as no reader tries to become a writer.

Now search your own code for .lock(). Each one should sit right before a try whose finally starts with unlock(). A lock() with no finally is waiting for its first exception.

Next, we'll take the optimistic idea further and change a balance with no lock at all. How can two threads update one number safely if neither ever waits?

sections.h: A lock that can give up: ReentrantLock, tryLock and lockInterruptibly
sections.html:
In synchronized and intrinsic locks, we pictured a lock as the key to the bank's vault: one door, one key, and a line of threads outside. synchronized gives that line no choices. A thread that joins it waits until the key comes back, however long that takes. It can't give up after a timeout. An interrupt, another thread's request that it stop, doesn't reach it until it holds the key.

ReentrantLock, from java.util.concurrent.locks, is the same vault with controls on the door. Like synchronized, it lets one thread in at a time, and the next owner sees every write the last owner made. It's reentrant too: the owner can take it again, and the lock counts the holds. Unlike synchronized, it gives a waiting thread choices:

  • tryLock() takes the lock only if it's free right now, and returns false otherwise.
  • tryLock(200, MILLISECONDS) waits at most 200 ms. The last lesson used it to break deadlocks, where threads wait for each other forever.
  • lockInterruptibly() waits, but leaves the line with InterruptedException when the thread is interrupted.
  • new ReentrantLock(true) makes a fair lock, which hands the lock to the thread that has waited longest.

TryLockDemo plays out the evening from the opening. The interest thread holds the ledger lock for 1.5 seconds. Older code in the bank still guards the ledger with synchronized, so the job also holds that monitor, the built-in lock every Java object has. Three threads want in. The cash-machine waits with tryLock(200 ms), the statement printer with lockInterruptibly(), and an old teller screen with synchronized. After 400 ms, the main thread prints two of their states and interrupts those two, as a shutdown would. Before you read the output, guess which of the three keeps waiting after it's interrupted:

cash-machine: gave up after 200 ms, asked the customer to try again
states: statement=WAITING, teller=BLOCKED
statement: interrupted while waiting, gave up cleanly
teller: got the monitor at last, interrupted=true

The cash machine waited exactly as long as we allowed, then gave its customer an answer. The statement printer left the line the moment it was interrupted. The teller heard nothing. It got the monitor after the full 1.5 seconds, and only then found out that someone had asked it to stop, more than a second earlier.

The two states differ, too. A thread waiting for a ReentrantLock is parked, which means put to sleep until another thread wakes it, so it shows WAITING. A thread waiting for a monitor shows BLOCKED. Expect WAITING (parking) when you read a thread dump (the printout of every thread's state) of code that uses explicit locks.

All that control has a price, the one the opening warned about. A synchronized block lets go when it exits, even when it throws. A ReentrantLock lets go only when you call unlock(). So every use follows one pattern. Here it guards the ledger's entries, the amounts paid in and out:

Java
private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();
private final List<Entry> entries = new ArrayList<>();   // the ledger's entries, guarded by lock

void post(Entry e) {
    lock.lock();               // before the try, never inside it
    try {
        entries.add(e);
    } finally {
        lock.unlock();         // first line of finally: runs even if add throws
    }
}
Kotlin
private val lock = ReentrantLock()
private val entries = mutableListOf<Entry>()       // the ledger's entries, guarded by lock

fun post(e: Entry) {
    lock.withLock {            // kotlin.concurrent: lock(), try, finally unlock()
        entries += e
    }
}

Read the Java version aloud: take the lock; try the work; finally, whatever happens, give the lock back. In Kotlin, withLock { } writes the lock(), the try and the finally for you.

Leave out the finally, and one rare exception, from a bad input say, skips the unlock(). The thread moves on with the lock still taken, and every thread after it parks in lock() for good. A thread dump then shows dozens of threads WAITING, while jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l names an owner that is busy somewhere else entirely.

A ReentrantLock lets go only when you tell it to. Put every unlock() in a finally.

My rule: use synchronized for a short, simple critical section (the code that runs under the lock), and switch to ReentrantLock when you need one of its controls. For ordinary code, the two cost about the same on current JDKs. One old reason to switch is mostly gone, too. A virtual thread is a very light thread that the JVM runs on top of an ordinary one. Before JDK 24, a virtual thread that blocked inside synchronized held on to that ordinary thread. JDK 24 fixed that in most cases (the change is called JEP 491), and the virtual threads track covers it.

The cash machine can give up now. But a lock is also a place to wait for something to change, as the cooks did in wait, notify and guarded blocks. There, too, ReentrantLock has something better.

try.title: Three ways to wait for a busy lock
steps: Read TryLockDemo. The interest thread holds the ledger lock and the old monitor for 1.5 seconds. cash-machine waits with tryLock(200 ms), statement with lockInterruptibly(), and teller with synchronized.
Predict the order of the four output lines, and the states printed for statement and teller.
Run it. Then let the cash machine wait 2 seconds instead of 200 ms, and run it again.

code.title: TryLockDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l07; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock; /** * The end-of-day interest job holds the ledger lock for 1.5 s. * Three threads want in, each in a different way. */ public class TryLockDemo { static final ReentrantLock ledger = new ReentrantLock(); static final Object monitor = new Object(); // older code still guards the ledger with this public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Thread interest = new Thread(() -> { ledger.lock(); try { synchronized (monitor) { // the job holds the lock AND the monitor pause(1_500); // adding interest to every account } } finally { ledger.unlock(); } }, "interest"); interest.start(); Thread.sleep(100); // let the interest job get in first Thread cashMachine = new Thread(() -> { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); try { if (ledger.tryLock(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) { // wait at most 200 ms try { System.out.println("cash-machine: got the lock"); } finally { ledger.unlock(); } } else { System.out.printf("cash-machine: gave up after %d ms, asked the customer to try again%n", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); } } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }, "cash-machine"); Thread statement = new Thread(() -> { try { ledger.lockInterruptibly(); // an interrupt can cancel this wait try { System.out.println("statement: got the lock"); } finally { ledger.unlock(); } } catch (InterruptedException e) { System.out.println("statement: interrupted while waiting, gave up cleanly"); } }, "statement"); Thread teller = new Thread(() -> { synchronized (monitor) { // no way to give up here System.out.println("teller: got the monitor at last, interrupted=" + Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()); } }, "teller"); cashMachine.start(); statement.start(); teller.start(); Thread.sleep(400); System.out.println("states: statement=" + statement.getState() + ", teller=" + teller.getState()); statement.interrupt(); // the program is shutting down teller.interrupt(); for (Thread t : new Thread[] {cashMachine, statement, teller, interest}) t.join(); } static void pause(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } }

try.expect: The cash machine gives up after about 200 ms. The states are statement=WAITING (parked on the lock) and teller=BLOCKED (waiting for a monitor). The interrupt ends the statement printer's wait at once. The teller keeps waiting until the interest job finishes, and only then sees interrupted=true. With a 2-second wait, the cash machine gets the lock as soon as the job is done.

aside.title: Why does lock() go before the try, and not inside it?
aside.html: Because the finally should run only when you really hold the lock. If lock() sat inside the try and something failed before the lock was taken, the finally would call unlock() on a lock you don't hold. unlock() then throws IllegalMonitorStateException, and that new exception hides the one that really went wrong. lockInterruptibly() is the call most likely to fail that way, when an interrupt arrives while it waits. The same goes for tryLock: call it before the try, and enter the try only when it returned true.

video.title: ReentrantLock is the same room with controls on the door: tryLock with a timeout and lockInterruptibly let a waiter leave, each Condition is its own waiting room, and readers share while the writer waits for an empty room

sections.h: One waiting room per reason to wait: Condition
sections.html:
Remember the kitchen from wait, notify and guarded blocks. Waiters clip order tickets to a rail, and cooks take them off. When the rail is full, waiters wait for a free slot. When it's empty, cooks wait for a ticket. A monitor has only one wait set, the group of threads waiting on it, so both kinds sat on the same bench. A notify() meant for a cook could wake a waiter instead, and that stalled the kitchen. So we woke everyone with notifyAll() and let each while loop decide.

A ReentrantLock can have as many benches as you like. Each one is a Condition: a queue of threads waiting for one particular change, made with lock.newCondition(). await() plays the part of wait(). It lets go of the lock, parks, and takes the lock back before it returns. signal() and signalAll() play notify() and notifyAll().

Let's rebuild the rail with two of them: notFull, where waiters wait for a free slot, and notEmpty, where cooks wait for a ticket. Here's the waiter's side, put:

Java
private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();
private final Condition notFull = lock.newCondition();    // waiters wait here for a free slot
private final Condition notEmpty = lock.newCondition();   // cooks wait here for a ticket

public void put(T ticket) throws InterruptedException {
    lock.lock();
    try {
        while (items.size() == capacity) notFull.await();   // lets go of the lock while waiting
        items.addLast(ticket);
        notEmpty.signal();                                   // wake one cook
    } finally {
        lock.unlock();
    }
}
Kotlin
private val lock = ReentrantLock()
private val notFull = lock.newCondition()      // waiters wait here for a free slot
private val notEmpty = lock.newCondition()     // cooks wait here for a ticket

fun put(ticket: T) = lock.withLock {
    while (items.size == capacity) notFull.await()   // lets go of the lock while waiting
    items.addLast(ticket)
    notEmpty.signal()                                 // wake one cook
}

First we take the lock. While the rail is full, we wait on notFull, which lets go of the lock until a cook signals. Then we clip the ticket on and signal notEmpty. Only cooks ever wait there, and one new ticket lets exactly one cook go on. Those are the two conditions under which the kitchen lesson said a single notify() is safe, and now they hold on each bench. So signal() is enough, and the other waiters sleep on.

Is it worth the trouble? WakeupCount measures it. Four waiters and four cooks move 20,000 tickets through a rail with room for one, twice. The first run uses one Condition with signalAll(), the kitchen lesson's design. The second uses two with signal(). Each run counts its wasted wake-ups, the times a thread woke, checked its loop, and had to wait again. One run printed:

one condition, signalAll():        wasted wake-ups:    88,340   (2175 ms)
notFull + notEmpty, signal():      wasted wake-ups:       375   (676 ms)

Both runs moved all 20,000 tickets. With one bench, every signalAll() woke all seven other threads, and most went straight back to sleep: 88,340 times. With two benches, that fell to 375, and the run took a third of the time. The Kotlin twin printed 93,684 against 3,155. The count isn't zero, because of barging: a running thread can grab the lock and the ticket before the signalled thread wakes up. That's why the while loop stays.

The rules from the kitchen still hold:

  • Call await() and signal() only while you hold the lock, or you get IllegalMonitorStateException.
  • Wait in a while loop. The Condition Javadoc (the official API documentation) allows spurious wake-ups, wake-ups with no signal at all. And another thread can take the ticket between the signal and your return.
  • Don't call wait() or notify() on a Condition. It's an object like any other, so notFull.wait() compiles. It uses the condition's own monitor, which you don't hold, and throws.

A Condition can also wait against a deadline. awaitNanos(n) waits at most n nanoseconds (billionths of a second) and returns the time left, so a loop can keep waiting for whatever remains. The lab's offer(item, timeout) uses it.

One kind of waiting thread per Condition lets signal() wake the right one. Keep the while loop anyway.

Waiters and cooks both change the rail, so they have to take turns. Many threads only read shared data, though, and readers never get in each other's way. Making them take turns anyway is a waste.

try.title: Count the wasted wake-ups
steps: Read WakeupCount. Four waiters and four cooks move 20,000 tickets through a rail with room for one: once with one Condition and signalAll(), once with two Conditions and signal().
A wake-up is wasted when a thread wakes, checks its while loop, and has to wait again. Predict which version wastes more, and roughly how many more.
Run it twice and compare the counts and the times.

code.title: WakeupCount.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l07; import java.util.ArrayDeque; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.locks.Condition; import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock; /** * The kitchen's rail with room for one ticket. 4 waiters (producers) and 4 cooks (consumers) * move 20,000 tickets through it, twice: once with one Condition and signalAll(), once with * notFull/notEmpty and signal(). A wake-up is "wasted" when the thread wakes, re-checks, * and has to wait again. */ public class WakeupCount { static final class Buffer { final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock(); final Condition notFull; final Condition notEmpty; final boolean shared; final ArrayDeque<Integer> items = new ArrayDeque<>(); long wasted; // guarded by lock Buffer(boolean oneCondition) { shared = oneCondition; notFull = lock.newCondition(); notEmpty = oneCondition ? notFull : lock.newCondition(); // same queue, or two } void put(int x) throws InterruptedException { lock.lock(); try { while (items.size() == 1) { notFull.await(); if (items.size() == 1) wasted++; // woke up for nothing } items.add(x); if (shared) notEmpty.signalAll(); else notEmpty.signal(); } finally { lock.unlock(); } } int take() throws InterruptedException { lock.lock(); try { while (items.isEmpty()) { notEmpty.await(); if (items.isEmpty()) wasted++; } int x = items.remove(); if (shared) notFull.signalAll(); else notFull.signal(); return x; } finally { lock.unlock(); } } } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { for (boolean one : new boolean[] {true, false}) { Buffer buffer = new Buffer(one); List<Thread> threads = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) { threads.add(new Thread(() -> { try { for (int n = 0; n < 5_000; n++) buffer.put(n); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } })); threads.add(new Thread(() -> { try { for (int n = 0; n < 5_000; n++) buffer.take(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } })); } long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (Thread t : threads) t.start(); for (Thread t : threads) t.join(); System.out.printf("%-34s wasted wake-ups: %,9d (%d ms)%n", one ? "one condition, signalAll():" : "notFull + notEmpty, signal():", buffer.wasted, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); } } }

A wake-up is "wasted" when the thread wakes, re-checks, // and has to wait again. private class CountingBuffer(private val shared: Boolean) { private val lock = ReentrantLock() private val notFull: Condition = lock.newCondition() private val notEmpty: Condition = if (shared) notFull else lock.newCondition() // same queue, or two private val items = ArrayDeque<Int>() var wasted = 0L // guarded by lock private set fun put(x: Int) = lock.withLock { while (items.size == 1) { notFull.await() if (items.size == 1) wasted++ // woke up for nothing } items.addLast(x) if (shared) notEmpty.signalAll() else notEmpty.signal() } fun take(): Int = lock.withLock { while (items.isEmpty()) { notEmpty.await() if (items.isEmpty()) wasted++ } val x = items.removeFirst() if (shared) notFull.signalAll() else notFull.signal() x } } fun main() { for (one in listOf(true, false)) { val buffer = CountingBuffer(one) val t0 = System.nanoTime() val threads = (1..4).flatMap { listOf( thread { repeat(5_000) { n -> buffer.put(n) } }, thread { repeat(5_000) { buffer.take() } }, ) } threads.forEach { it.join() } val label = if (one) "one condition, signalAll():" else "notFull + notEmpty, signal():" println("%-34s wasted wake-ups: %,9d (%d ms)".format(label, buffer.wasted, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000)) } }

try.expect: With one condition, tens of thousands of wake-ups are wasted (88,340 and 93,684 in runs here), because every signalAll() wakes all seven other threads and most of them go back to sleep. With two conditions, the count drops to hundreds or a few thousand, and the run takes about a third or a quarter of the time. It isn't zero, because a running thread can barge in and take the ticket before the signalled thread wakes. That's why the while loop stays.

sections.h: Many readers, one writer: ReadWriteLock, and the upgrade that hangs
sections.html:
The bank keeps a table of exchange rates. For each currency pair, such as EURUSD, it says how many dollars one euro costs. Every cash machine and every teller reads it, about 5,000 times a second, and a refresh job replaces the rates every five seconds. Behind a plain lock, each reader waits for every other reader, though reading changes nothing.

Picture a reading room in a library. Anyone may come in and read, as many people at once as like. Rearranging the shelves is different: the librarian waits until the room is empty, then works alone with the door shut. A ReentrantReadWriteLock is that room. It has two locks inside. Many threads can hold the read lock together. The write lock is exclusive: it waits until no reader and no writer is inside, and while it's held, nobody else gets in:

Java
private final ReentrantReadWriteLock rw = new ReentrantReadWriteLock();
private final Map<String, BigDecimal> rates = new HashMap<>();   // guarded by rw

BigDecimal rate(String pair) {
    rw.readLock().lock();                 // many threads can hold this at once
    try {
        return rates.get(pair);
    } finally {
        rw.readLock().unlock();
    }
}

void refresh(Map<String, BigDecimal> fresh) {
    rw.writeLock().lock();                // waits until no reader and no writer holds the lock
    try {
        rates.clear();
        rates.putAll(fresh);
    } finally {
        rw.writeLock().unlock();
    }
}
Kotlin
private val rw = ReentrantReadWriteLock()
private val rates = HashMap<String, BigDecimal>()    // guarded by rw

fun rate(pair: String): BigDecimal? = rw.read {     // many threads can hold this at once
    rates[pair]
}

fun refresh(fresh: Map<String, BigDecimal>) = rw.write {   // waits until no reader and no writer holds the lock
    rates.clear()
    rates.putAll(fresh)
}

Readers share the room, and the refresh works alone. The trap is a missing rate. The table is a cache, a store of answers kept close at hand, and a pair that isn't in it yet is called a cache miss. The natural code checks under the read lock and, if the rate is missing, takes the write lock to load it:

Java
// Naive: hangs the first time a pair is missing
rw.readLock().lock();
try {
    BigDecimal r = rates.get(pair);
    if (r != null) return r;
    rw.writeLock().lock();         // waits for every reader to leave, this thread included: forever
    try {
        r = loader.apply(pair);
        rates.put(pair, r);
        return r;
    } finally {
        rw.writeLock().unlock();
    }
} finally {
    rw.readLock().unlock();
}
Kotlin
// Naive: hangs the first time a pair is missing
rw.readLock().lock()
try {
    val r = rates[pair]
    if (r != null) return r
    rw.writeLock().lock()         // waits for every reader to leave, this thread included: forever
    try {
        return loader(pair).also { rates[pair] = it }
    } finally {
        rw.writeLock().unlock()
    }
} finally {
    rw.readLock().unlock()
}

Asking for the write lock while you still hold the read lock is called an upgrade, and ReentrantReadWriteLock doesn't support it. The write lock waits for every reader to leave. This thread is a reader, and it won't leave until it gets the write lock. So it waits, very patiently, for itself. In the reading room, it's a reader who decides to rearrange the shelves and waits inside for the room to empty. Two threads that try it at once wait for each other.

The thread dump won't point it out, either. Run UpgradeDeadlock with -Pargs=hang and ask for a dump with jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l. On JDK 21, main looks like this, trimmed:

"main" #1 ... waiting on condition
   java.lang.Thread.State: WAITING (parking)
	at jdk.internal.misc.Unsafe.park(java.base@21.0.12.1/Native Method)
	- parking to wait for  <0x0000000737818bc0> (a java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantReadWriteLock$NonfairSync)
	...
	at java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantReadWriteLock$WriteLock.lock(java.base@21.0.12.1/ReentrantReadWriteLock.java:959)
	at workbench.concurrency.l07.UpgradeDeadlock.main(UpgradeDeadlock.java:22)

   Locked ownable synchronizers:
	- None

There's no Found one Java-level deadlock, and the list of locks that main owns is empty. A read lock has no single owner, so the JVM's deadlock detector has no cycle to find. It's a deadlock with one thread in it, and nobody reports it.

The fix has three steps: let go of the read lock, take the write lock, and check again. The check matters, because another thread may have loaded the rate while you held nothing. The lab's FxRateCache needs exactly that. Going the other way, a downgrade, is allowed: while holding the write lock, take the read lock, then let go of the write lock.

A read lock never turns into a write lock. Let go first, then check again under the write lock.

A read-write lock pays off when reads are frequent and take a while, and writes are rare. For a map lookup that takes 50 nanoseconds, its extra bookkeeping can cost more than it saves. And when the refresh replaces the whole table at once, a map that never changes, held in a volatile field (one whose reads always see the latest write), needs no lock at all. Lesson 11 of this track shows that pattern.

The read lock still writes to memory, though: every reader adds one to its count on the way in. On a very busy path, that one write is the next cost to go.

try.title: Upgrade, then downgrade
steps: Run UpgradeDeadlock. It tries the upgrade with tryLock(1, SECONDS) so it can't hang, then does a downgrade.
Run the Kotlin twin. Its last line puts write { } inside read { }. Predict: does it hang?
Optional: run the Java one with -Pargs=hang. In a second terminal, run jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l with the printed PID and find main. Stop it with Ctrl+C.

code.title: UpgradeDeadlock.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l07; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantReadWriteLock; /** * One thread, one ReentrantReadWriteLock. Upgrading (read, then write) never succeeds. * Downgrading (write, then read, then release the write) is allowed. * Run with -Pargs=hang to use lock() instead of tryLock() and see the thread wait forever. */ public class UpgradeDeadlock { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { ReentrantReadWriteLock rw = new ReentrantReadWriteLock(); boolean hang = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("hang"); // 1. the "upgrade": ask for the write lock while still holding the read lock rw.readLock().lock(); try { System.out.println("holding the read lock, read holds = " + rw.getReadHoldCount()); if (hang) { System.out.println("calling writeLock().lock() ... (pid " + ProcessHandle.current().pid() + ", Ctrl+C to stop)"); rw.writeLock().lock(); // waits for every reader to leave, us included } boolean got = rw.writeLock().tryLock(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS); // the same wait, with a time limit System.out.println("write lock while holding a read lock, after 1 s: " + got); } finally { rw.readLock().unlock(); } // 2. the downgrade: write lock, then read lock, then let go of the write lock rw.writeLock().lock(); try { rw.readLock().lock(); // allowed: we are the only writer } finally { rw.writeLock().unlock(); } try { System.out.println("downgraded: write locked = " + rw.isWriteLocked() + ", read holds = " + rw.getReadHoldCount()); } finally { rw.readLock().unlock(); } } }

alt.title: UpgradeDeadlock.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l07 import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantReadWriteLock import kotlin.concurrent.read import kotlin.concurrent.write // One thread, one ReentrantReadWriteLock. Upgrading (read, then write) never succeeds. // Downgrading (write, then read, then release the write) is allowed. // Run with -Pargs=hang to use lock() instead of tryLock() and see the thread wait forever. fun main(args: Array<String>) { val rw = ReentrantReadWriteLock() val hang = args.firstOrNull() == "hang" // 1. the "upgrade": ask for the write lock while still holding the read lock rw.readLock().lock() try { println("holding the read lock, read holds = ${rw.readHoldCount}") if (hang) { println("calling writeLock().lock() ... (pid ${ProcessHandle.current().pid()}, Ctrl+C to stop)") rw.writeLock().lock() // waits for every reader to leave, us included } val got = rw.writeLock().tryLock(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS) // the same wait, with a time limit println("write lock while holding a read lock, after 1 s: $got") } finally { rw.readLock().unlock() } // 2. the downgrade: write lock, then read lock, then let go of the write lock rw.writeLock().lock() try { rw.readLock().lock() // allowed: we are the only writer } finally { rw.writeLock().unlock() } try { println("downgraded: write locked = ${rw.isWriteLocked}, read holds = ${rw.readHoldCount}") } finally { rw.readLock().unlock() } // 3. Kotlin only: write {} inside read {} does not hang, because write {} first lets go of // this thread's read locks. That makes it a release-then-acquire, not an atomic upgrade. rw.read { rw.write { println("kotlin write {} inside read {}: write locked = ${rw.isWriteLocked}, read holds = ${rw.readHoldCount}") } } }

try.expect: write lock while holding a read lock, after 1 s: false, then downgraded: write locked = false, read holds = 1. The Kotlin write { } inside read { } doesn't hang: it prints write locked = true, read holds = 0, because Kotlin's write lets go of this thread's read locks first. With -Pargs=hang, the dump shows main parked in WriteLock.lock and no deadlock report.

sections.h: Reading with no lock at all: StampedLock and the optimistic read
sections.html:
Every reader of a read lock adds one to the lock's count, and takes one away on the way out. On a machine with many cores, that count lives in one cache line. A cache line is the small block of memory that a core copies into its own fast memory, its cache. A core must own the line before it can write to it. So every reader pulls the line over to its own core, and the line bounces from core to core.

StampedLock (JDK 8) adds a mode that writes nothing at all, the optimistic read. Read it as "go ahead and read, then check whether anyone wrote while you did". The rate table shows two prices for the euro: the bank buys euros at one price and sells them 2 cents higher. A reader must never see a new buying price with an old selling price:

Java
long stamp = lock.tryOptimisticRead();   // 1. no lock, just a version number
long b = buy, s = sell;                  // 2. copy both prices into locals
if (!lock.validate(stamp)) {             // 3. a writer got in: the copies may be torn
    stamp = lock.readLock();             // 4. fall back to a real read lock
    try { b = buy; s = sell; } finally { lock.unlockRead(stamp); }
}
return new EuroPrices(b, s);             // 5. use the locals only after validate
Kotlin
var stamp = lock.tryOptimisticRead()     // 1. no lock, just a version number
var b = buy; var s = sell                // 2. copy both prices into locals
if (!lock.validate(stamp)) {             // 3. a writer got in: the copies may be torn
    stamp = lock.readLock()              // 4. fall back to a real read lock
    try { b = buy; s = sell } finally { lock.unlockRead(stamp) }
}
return EuroPrices(b, s)                  // 5. use the locals only after validate

tryOptimisticRead() returns a stamp, a version number of the lock (or 0 if a writer holds it). We copy both prices into locals with no lock held. Then validate(stamp) asks: did any writer get in since that stamp? If not, the two copies belong together. If one did, we throw them away and read again under a real read lock.

Between the stamp and the check, the copies can be torn: half old and half new, such as a new buying price with an old selling price. The Javadoc promises sound values only if a later validate returns true. So the code in between must not act on them: no loops driven by them, no array index, no calls that could throw.

An optimistic read can be torn. Copy, validate, and only then use.

OptimisticRead checks that promise. A writer keeps moving both prices, and a reader reads them optimistically for one second. One run printed:

reads: 843,481   failed validate(): 22,969   torn pairs caught: 12,960   torn pairs that passed validate(): 0

About one read in 37 failed to validate, and more than half of those had really caught a torn pair. Not one torn pair got past validate().

The speed comes without the safety rails of the other locks:

  • StampedLock is not reentrant. A thread that holds the write lock and asks for it again waits for itself, which makes it the second lock in this lesson that can.
  • It has no Conditions.
  • A stamp isn't tied to a thread, and you must pass the right stamp to unlockRead or unlockWrite.

Use it for a few fields that are read on a very busy path and written rarely, like these two prices. Even then, wait until a profiler, a tool that measures where a program spends its time, shows that the read-write lock is the cost. For most code, ReentrantReadWriteLock, or no lock at all, is the better choice.

That's where this lesson's tools stop. Each one still makes some thread wait for a lock, or fall back to one when its optimism fails. For a single number, such as one balance, there's a way to change it safely with no lock at all.

try.title: Catch torn reads with validate()
steps: Read OptimisticRead. A writer keeps moving the bank's two euro prices, and once a write is done the selling price is always the buying price plus 2. The reader counts the optimistic reads that saw a pair where that isn't true.
Predict: will any torn pair get past validate()?
Run it. Then delete the validate check (treat every optimistic read as good) and count the torn pairs that would have reached the caller.

code.title: OptimisticRead.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l07; import java.util.concurrent.locks.StampedLock; /** * The bank's two prices for the euro: it buys at one price and sells 2 cents higher. * A writer keeps moving both prices. A reader reads them optimistically for one second * and counts how often validate() caught a half-written pair. */ public class OptimisticRead { static final StampedLock lock = new StampedLock(); static long buy = 100, sell = 102; // guarded by lock; sell == buy + 2 when no write is in progress static volatile boolean done; public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Thread writer = new Thread(() -> { long v = 100; while (!done) { long stamp = lock.writeLock(); try { buy = ++v; for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++) Thread.onSpinWait(); // widens the half-written moment sell = v + 2; } finally { lock.unlockWrite(stamp); } } }); writer.start(); long reads = 0, failed = 0, tornCaught = 0, tornPassed = 0; long end = System.nanoTime() + 1_000_000_000L; while (System.nanoTime() < end) { reads++; long stamp = lock.tryOptimisticRead(); // 1. no lock taken, just a version number long b = buy, s = sell; // 2. copy the fields into locals boolean torn = s - b != 2; if (lock.validate(stamp)) { // 3. did a writer get in since step 1? if (torn) tornPassed++; // never happens } else { failed++; if (torn) tornCaught++; stamp = lock.readLock(); // 4. fall back to a real read lock try { b = buy; s = sell; } finally { lock.unlockRead(stamp); } } } done = true; writer.join(); System.out.printf("reads: %,d failed validate(): %,d torn pairs caught: %,d torn pairs that passed validate(): %d%n", reads, failed, tornCaught, tornPassed); } }

alt.title: OptimisticRead.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l07 import java.util.concurrent.locks.StampedLock import kotlin.concurrent.thread // The bank's two prices for the euro: it buys at one price and sells 2 cents higher. // A writer keeps moving both prices. A reader reads them optimistically for one second // and counts how often validate() caught a half-written pair. private class EuroPrices { val lock = StampedLock() var buy = 100L // guarded by lock; sell == buy + 2 when no write is in progress var sell = 102L } @Volatile private var done = false fun main() { val q = EuroPrices() val writer = thread { var v = 100L while (!done) { val stamp = q.lock.writeLock() try { q.buy = ++v repeat(20) { Thread.onSpinWait() } // widens the half-written moment q.sell = v + 2 } finally { q.lock.unlockWrite(stamp) } } } var reads = 0L; var failed = 0L; var tornCaught = 0L; var tornPassed = 0L val end = System.nanoTime() + 1_000_000_000L while (System.nanoTime() < end) { reads++ var stamp = q.lock.tryOptimisticRead() // 1. no lock taken, just a version number var b = q.buy; var s = q.sell // 2. copy the fields into locals val torn = s - b != 2L if (q.lock.validate(stamp)) { // 3. did a writer get in since step 1? if (torn) tornPassed++ // never happens } else { failed++ if (torn) tornCaught++ stamp = q.lock.readLock() // 4. fall back to a real read lock try { b = q.buy; s = q.sell } finally { q.lock.unlockRead(stamp) } } } done = true writer.join() println("reads: %,d failed validate(): %,d torn pairs caught: %,d torn pairs that passed validate(): %d" .format(reads, failed, tornCaught, tornPassed)) }

try.expect: Tens of thousands of reads fail validation in the second (22,969 of 843,481 in one run here), and more than half of those saw a torn pair, a new buying price with an old selling price. The last number, torn pairs that passed validate(), is always 0. Without the check, every one of those torn pairs would have gone to the caller.

compare.title: A read-mostly cache in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Java
java.html: BigDecimal rate(String pair) { rw.readLock().lock(); try { BigDecimal r = rates.get(pair); if (r != null) return r; // 1. fast path under the read lock } finally { rw.readLock().unlock(); // 2. let go BEFORE asking for the write lock } rw.writeLock().lock(); try { return rates.computeIfAbsent(pair, loader); // 3. check again under the write lock } finally { rw.writeLock().unlock(); } }

kotlin.title: Kotlin
kotlin.html: fun rate(pair: String): BigDecimal = rw.read { rates[pair] ?: rw.write { // write {} let go of our read lock first, so another thread may have loaded it: check again rates.getOrPut(pair) { loader(pair) } } }

compare.note: The Java version must let go of the read lock before it takes the write lock, or it hangs. The Kotlin version looks like an upgrade, and it doesn't hang, because the standard library's ReentrantReadWriteLock.write releases every read lock this thread holds, takes the write lock, and takes the read locks back afterwards. Its documentation warns that this is not an atomic upgrade: another thread can write in the gap, so anything you checked before write must be checked again inside it. That's why both versions check again (computeIfAbsent, getOrPut). Kotlin's helpers remove the ceremony of lock, try and finally. They don't remove the reasoning.

worked.title: A lock per account that gives up

steps.say: Each account's changes must run one at a time, because each one checks and then updates that account's balance. Changes to different accounts must not wait for each other. And if one thread gets stuck while holding an account, other requests for that account should give up after a short wait and ask the caller to try again, instead of piling up behind it. Read the solution and its subgoal labels.
steps.code: class AccountLocks { private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, ReentrantLock> locks = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); <T> T withAccount(String accountId, Duration maxWait, Supplier<T> action) throws InterruptedException { // 1. one lock per account, created at most once ReentrantLock lock = locks.computeIfAbsent(accountId, id -> new ReentrantLock()); // 2. wait a bounded time; an interrupt also ends the wait if (!lock.tryLock(maxWait.toNanos(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)) { throw new AccountBusyException(accountId); // 3. busy: give up, the caller tries again later } try { return action.get(); // 4. critical section } finally { lock.unlock(); // 5. always release } } }

alt.html: class AccountLocks { private val locks = ConcurrentHashMap<String, ReentrantLock>() fun <T> withAccount(accountId: String, maxWait: Duration, action: () -> T): T { // 1. one lock per account, created at most once val lock = locks.computeIfAbsent(accountId) { ReentrantLock() } // 2. wait a bounded time; an interrupt also ends the wait if (!lock.tryLock(maxWait.toNanos(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)) { throw AccountBusyException(accountId) // 3. busy: give up, the caller tries again later } try { return action() // 4. critical section } finally { lock.unlock() // 5. always release } } }

steps.say: Before reading on, explain to yourself: why does tryLock sit outside the try, when unlock() is inside the finally? Answer: if tryLock returns false or throws InterruptedException, this thread doesn't hold the lock. A finally that called unlock() would throw IllegalMonitorStateException and hide the real result. Only the code that runs while you hold the lock goes inside the try.

Why not synchronized (accountId)? Two Strings with the same letters are often different objects, so two requests for the same account could each lock their own string and run together. Interned strings, the single shared copy Java keeps of each string literal, go the other way: unrelated code that locks the same literal shares your lock, as synchronized and intrinsic locks showed. And synchronized has no timeout. A map of real lock objects avoids all three problems.

One problem remains: the map gains a lock for every account it ever sees, and never shrinks. With millions of accounts, that's memory you don't get back. Removing entries safely is harder than it looks, because another thread may be about to lock the entry you remove. The usual answer is lock striping: a fixed array of locks, with each account mapped to one of them by its hash.
steps.code: private final ReentrantLock[] stripes = new ReentrantLock[256]; { for (int i = 0; i < stripes.length; i++) stripes[i] = new ReentrantLock(); } ReentrantLock lockFor(String accountId) { return stripes[Math.floorMod(accountId.hashCode(), stripes.length)]; // two accounts may share a stripe: fine }

alt.html: private val stripes = Array(256) { ReentrantLock() } fun lockFor(accountId: String): ReentrantLock = stripes[Math.floorMod(accountId.hashCode(), stripes.size)] // two accounts may share a stripe: fine

steps.say: Two accounts that share a stripe now wait for each other. That costs a little speed and nothing in correctness. If you ever hold two account locks at once, for a transfer, take the stripes in index order, as in Deadlock, livelock and starvation, and skip the second lock when both accounts land on the same stripe.

lab.title: A rail with two conditions and a rate table that doesn't hang
steps: Run the tests. All eight fail. The five LockBuffer tests hit UnsupportedOperationException. Two FxRateCache tests time out (the upgrade hang), and the snapshot test finds rates from two different refreshes mixed together.

Part 1: LockBuffer is the kitchen's rail from the second section, for any kind of item. Write it with one ReentrantLock and two Conditions, notFull and notEmpty. Check the capacity in the constructor. put and take follow the shape in the second section, with signal().
Write offer(item, timeout): the same as put, but wait with notFull.awaitNanos(remaining) and return false when the time runs out.

Part 2: FxRateCache is the bank's exchange-rate table from the third section. Fix rate: let go of the read lock, take the write lock, and check again before calling the loader, so the loader runs once per currency pair.
Fix snapshot so it reads every pair under one read lock. Run the tests until all eight pass, then twice more.
hints: awaitNanos returns the nanoseconds still left (zero or less when time is up). Keep the returned value and pass it to the next awaitNanos in the loop.
Use lock.lockInterruptibly() at the top of put, take and offer, so an interrupted thread doesn't wait for the lock either. await() already throws InterruptedException when interrupted.
The cache's HashMap is fine as it is: every access to it happens under the read or the write lock. Only the order in which you take the locks is wrong.
lab.done: All eight tests in ExplicitLocksTest pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: Two conditions from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write a bounded buffer, the kitchen's rail, with a ReentrantLock and two Conditions: put waits while it's full, take waits while it's empty. Then check your work: is every unlock() in a finally, every await() in a while, and does each method signal the other side's condition?

answer.html: class Buffer<T> { private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock(); private final Condition notFull = lock.newCondition(); private final Condition notEmpty = lock.newCondition(); private final Deque<T> items = new ArrayDeque<>(); private final int capacity; Buffer(int capacity) { this.capacity = capacity; } void put(T item) throws InterruptedException { lock.lock(); try { while (items.size() == capacity) notFull.await(); items.addLast(item); notEmpty.signal(); } finally { lock.unlock(); } } T take() throws InterruptedException { lock.lock(); try { while (items.isEmpty()) notEmpty.await(); T head = items.removeFirst(); notFull.signal(); return head; } finally { lock.unlock(); } } }

alt.title: Kotlin
alt.html: class Buffer<T>(private val capacity: Int) { private val lock = ReentrantLock() private val notFull = lock.newCondition() private val notEmpty = lock.newCondition() private val items = ArrayDeque<T>() fun put(item: T) = lock.withLock { while (items.size == capacity) notFull.await() items.addLast(item) notEmpty.signal() } fun take(): T = lock.withLock { while (items.isEmpty()) notEmpty.await() items.removeFirst().also { notFull.signal() } } }

recap: ReentrantLock lets one thread in at a time and makes its writes visible, like synchronized, but you release it yourself: lock() right before try, unlock() first in finally, or Kotlin's withLock.
Reach for it when a waiting thread needs a choice: tryLock with a timeout, lockInterruptibly, a fair lock, or more than one condition.
Each Condition is its own waiting room. With one per kind of waiting thread, signal() is enough. Still wait in a while loop.
A read-write lock lets readers share. Asking for the write lock while you hold the read lock waits forever, and the deadlock detector won't report it. Let go, take the write lock, check again.
StampedLock's optimistic read takes no lock: copy into locals, validate, and only then use the values. It isn't reentrant.
The limit: every tool here still makes threads wait for a lock, or fall back to one. For a single number, the next lesson changes it with no lock at all.

explain.prompt: A teammate asks: "Should we replace all our synchronized blocks with ReentrantLock? I heard it's faster." Explain what you would tell them.
explain.answer: Not by default. Both let one thread in at a time and make its writes visible to the next owner, and on current JDKs they cost about the same for ordinary code. synchronized can't leak: it lets go on every exit. With ReentrantLock you must release it in a finally, and one missed path holds the lock forever. I'd switch only where we need something synchronized can't do: give up after a timeout with tryLock, let an interrupt cancel the wait with lockInterruptibly, use a fair lock, or have separate conditions for different kinds of waiting threads. For data that is read far more than it's written, I'd look at a read-write lock, or better, a snapshot that never changes behind a volatile reference.

deeper.html:
ReentrantLock, ReentrantReadWriteLock, Semaphore and CountDownLatch are all built on one class, AbstractQueuedSynchronizer (AQS). It keeps one int of state and a queue of waiting threads. For ReentrantLock the state is the hold count; for a semaphore it is the number of permits left; for a latch it is the count. A thread that can't go on joins the queue and parks with LockSupport.park. That's why it shows as WAITING in a dump, with a line like parking to wait for <0x...> (a java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock$NonfairSync). A release unparks the next thread in the queue.

In non-fair mode, the default, a thread that arrives just as the lock is released can take it before the queued thread wakes. That's barging, and it's why the two-condition rail in the second Try it still wasted some wake-ups. It's also why non-fair locks get through far more work: waking a parked thread takes microseconds, and a running thread can take and release the lock many times in that gap. Fair mode closes the gap and pays the wake-up cost on every hand-off. Even on a fair lock, the untimed tryLock() barges: its Javadoc says it does not honor the fairness setting.

ReentrantReadWriteLock splits its 32-bit state into two 16-bit halves, one for read holds and one for write holds. That's why its Javadoc caps it at 65,535 recursive write locks and 65,535 read locks.

StampedLock also has tryConvertToWriteLock(stamp), which upgrades a read or optimistic stamp to a write stamp if no other thread is in the way, and returns 0 if it can't. It's the only upgrade among the JDK's locks, and it can fail, so you still need the fallback path.

If you ever build your own synchronizer, subclass AQS and implement tryAcquire and tryRelease; its Javadoc has a small Mutex example. First check java.util.concurrent for one that already exists. Lesson 10 of this track covers the common ones.
